entries.task_id: kituba|is|spoken in the southern part of the republic of congo
entries.description: Kituba is spoken in the southern part of the Republic of Congo
entries.subject: Kituba
entries.object: spoken in the southern part of the Republic of Congo

spans.text: Bantu-based Kikongo-Kituba is spoken in the southern part of the Republic of Congo, in the southwestern part of the Democratic Republic of Congo, and in the northern part of Angola (see Map 1).

entries.task_id: it|is|lexified primarily by kimanyanga
entries.description: It is lexified primarily by Kimanyanga
entries.subject: It
entries.object: lexified primarily by Kimanyanga

spans.text: It is lexified primarily by Kimanyanga, a member of the Kikongo language cluster (Bantu H16), which was already functioning as a major trade language by the time the colonization of the Congo (the present Democratic Republic of Congo) started in the late 19th century.

entries.task_id: kimanyanga|was|adopted as the labourers’ lingua franca
entries.description: Kimanyanga was adopted as the labourers’ lingua franca
entries.subject: Kimanyanga
entries.object: adopted as the labourers’ lingua franca

spans.text: (Kikongo‑)Kimanyanga was adopted as the labourers’ lingua franca.

entries.task_id: of early|colonial|administration posts west
entries.description: of early colonial administration posts west
entries.subject: of early
entries.object: administration posts west

spans.text: (The reasons for this evolution are articulated below.) Gradually, it emerged as the vernacular of early colonial administration posts west, south, and east of Kinshasa (while Lingala was expanding from the North into Kinshasa and would eventually drive “Kikongo” out of the colonial capital), thanks to the colonial auxiliaries, who accompanied the colonizers and acted as their interpreters, and to the merchants and Christian missionaries.

entries.description: as a colonial lingua franca
entries.subject: as a
entries.object: lingua franca

spans.text: The geographical location of the Kongo Kingdom (see lower shaded area on Map 2) as the gateway of colonial expeditions into the hinterlands must have been an important factor favoring the adoption of Kimanyanga as a colonial lingua franca.

entries.description: daily maintenance is another relevant factor
entries.subject: daily maintenance
entries.object: another relevant factor

spans.text: The need for the exogenous labour force to communicate with the local population and buy goods from them for their daily maintenance is another relevant factor.

entries.task_id: which|identify|the language as kikongo
entries.description: which identify the language as Kikongo
entries.subject: which
entries.object: the language as Kikongo

spans.text: Noteworthy in this particular case are studies such as Ngalasso (1984, 1989, 1993), which identify the language as Kikongo, the prevailing name among its native speakers outside the Bakongo region, particularly in the Bandundu region, east and south of Kinshasa.

spans.text: The latter name appears to be associated with the mission of Kisantu, in the Lower Congo region, where the oldest senior seminary was situated and scholastic materials were produced by the Jesuit fathers.

entries.task_id: term bakongo|is|not used for speakers of kikongo-kituba
entries.description: term Bakongo is not used for speakers of Kikongo-Kituba
entries.subject: term Bakongo
entries.object: not used for speakers of Kikongo-Kituba

spans.text: Interestingly, the term Bakongo is not used for speakers of Kikongo-Kituba, apparently because of its origins as a lingua franca between populations speaking their own separate ethnic vernaculars and maintaining their diverse ethnic identities.

there|is|no single unified kikongo language spoken by the latter
entries.description:
that
there is no single unified Kikongo language spoken by the latter
entries.subject:
that
there
entries.object: no single unified Kikongo language spoken by the latter

spans.text: Kikongo-Kituba’s (native) speakers outside the Bakongo area do not think they speak the same language as the “Bakongo”, regardless of whether or not they are aware that there is no single unified Kikongo language spoken by the latter.

entries.task_id: and christian|missionaries|who invented a “bakongo” ethnic group
entries.description: and Christian missionaries who invented a “Bakongo” ethnic group
entries.subject: and Christian
entries.object: who invented a “Bakongo” ethnic group

spans.text: They are caught in a perversion created by the colonial administrators and Christian missionaries who invented a “Bakongo” ethnic group, perhaps by association with the precolonial Kongo Kingdom, and spread a derivative of Kimanyanga, under the same Kikongo label, into the Kwango-Kwilu area, where it was more meaningfully adopted as the natural name for the new “language” brought to the region by the Europeans and their auxiliaries.
